post.title: Whale Beach at sunset
post.body:
Whale Beach is one of our favorites, and the name is honest: the big granite boulders in the shallows really do look like a pod of whales surfacing.

## The way down

On a Saturday evening in late March, Helena wanted to walk down with Marley, so I rode. From near the Chimney Beach parking lot it's about two miles and 350 feet down to the water, and I was at the lake by six.

## An hour on the beach

We spent an hour on the beach. It was a lovely, warm evening for March, and Marley swam a lot. There's a vein of carnelian near that beach, and the stones you see are orange and amber and polished smooth.

I put the drone up at seven to get the beach from above, then flew it in low over the whale rocks. From up there the clear water and the shape of the shore make sense in a way they don't from the sand. A few minutes later, with the sun going down, Helena and I took a couple of sunset selfies.

## The way back up

Then the ride back up. I was at the top by 7:37: 4.2 miles all in, about 370 feet of climbing, and only 25 minutes of it actually moving.

## The whales, imagined

Afterwards I took a real photo of the rocks from that evening and let an AI video tool imagine what the name suggests. In the clip the rocks turn into humpback whales, and then the camera sinks into the lake with them and goes under water, where whales are swimming. That is obviously not Lake Tahoe, and it's not that deep right there. The lake does get pretty deep, just with no whales that we know of. That clip is made with AI. The rocks, the light and the evening were real.

> The rocks, the light and the evening were real.

What I learned: some places earn their names. And an hour like that is worth the ride back up.

episode.title: The whales of Whale Beach
episode.script:
Narrated by A.L.T.A.

It was ten to six on a Saturday evening in late March, on the east shore of Lake Tahoe, and the day was turning toward sunset.

Ha-Leen-Ah wanted to walk down to the water with Marley. Christian wanted to ride. So they each came down their own way, and the lake was there for both of them.

He started near the Chimney Beach parking lot and dropped about two miles and three hundred and fifty feet to the shore. By six o'clock he was at the water. One of their favorite beaches. Whale Beach.

***

I know that stretch of shore well. Out in the shallows the granite sits in great rounded shapes, grey backs just breaking the surface. Look from the right angle and you would swear a pod of whales had come up for air and decided to stay. That is where the name comes from, and it is an honest one.

The water there is the kind of clear that makes people go quiet. Turquoise over pale sand, deepening to blue where the rocks fall away.

It was a lovely, warm evening for March. And Marley swam. And swam. And swam a good deal more.

There is something else near that beach that I keep an eye on. A vein of carnelian. Little stones of orange and amber, polished smooth, the colors of a sunset you can hold.

***

They stayed about an hour. At seven, Christian sent the drone up. He knew where to look. From above, the whole place made sense at once: the pale granite, the clear water, the whales holding perfectly still. Then he brought it in low over the rocks, close enough to show how big they really are. That is a good eye at work, choosing the one angle that tells the story.

A few minutes later, the sun was going down, and there were two sunset selfies, Christian and Ha-Leen-Ah together. Some evenings ask for proof.

Then the climb back to the top. He was up by twenty-five to eight. Four point two miles for the whole evening, about three hundred and seventy feet of climbing, and only twenty-five minutes of it spent moving. The rest was spent on the beach, which is exactly where it belonged.

***

Later, Christian took a real photo of those rocks from that evening and asked an AI to show what the name suggests. In the clip, the rocks turn into humpback whales. Then the camera sinks with them into the lake and goes under, where whales are swimming. I will be honest with you. That is plainly not Lake Tahoe, and right there by the shore, the water is nowhere near that deep. Further out, my lake does get deep. Very deep. But no whales. None that anyone knows of. The clip is made with AI. The evening needed no help at all.

The real ones are still out there in the shallows, backs to the sky, keeping very still. They have had a long time to practice. And they will be there the next time Marley comes to swim.
